New office development in Apac becoming more selective; Singapore among markets facing constraints
article:
New development in the Asia Pacific (Apac) office market is becoming more selective as higher construction costs, elevated borrowing costs and lack of new supply challenge viability, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

In a November research report titled Global Office Supply: The Development Drought, the firm highlights a global slowdown in office development activity.

It estimates around 580 million sq ft of office space under construction globally in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 45% shortfall compared to the 3Q2017 peak of 1.04 billion sq ft. This puts global office development at its lowest level in a decade.

Cushman & Wakefield attribute the drop in new office construction to “higher for longer” interest rates and soaring construction costs stemming from trade disruptions related to the Suez Canal blockage and geopolitical tensions.

In its report, Cushman & Wakefield examined the viability of office markets across the globe by measuring economic rent: the minimum rent a new office development needs to earn to be profitable, after factoring land acquisition and development costs, operational costs, the developer’s margin, and borrowing costs.

“Comparing economic rent with prime market rent shows how close a market is to viability, and therefore to unlocking new supply,” the firm explains. Market rent on par or exceeding economic rent indicates an office market viable for new developments.

In Apac, the average economic rent is currently about 1% below prime market rents. By 2030, Cushman & Wakefield expect economic rent to exceed market rent by about 7%, implying limited viability for future developments across the region.

However, beyond the headline figures, viability diverges between individual markets, notes Dr Dominic Brown, head of international research and Global Think Tank at Cushman & Wakefield.

Major office markets in Apac, including Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney are seeing viability becoming more constrained as development economics “come under increasing pressure”, says Brown.

In contrast, Seoul and Bengaluru have emerged as standout markets for new supply, supported by strong occupier demand and rental growth.

In Singapore, prime market rents have largely tracked economic rents since 2023, according to the report. The trend is expected to continue until 2028, after which new Grade A supply from developments such as The Clifford, The Skywaters and One Comcentre , will test market absorption for backfill space.

While development opportunities "remain viable" in Singapore in the near term, Cushman & Wakefield expects future Grade A supply to be driven by redevelopment of older stock rather than fresh projects.

For Tokyo, prime market rents are currently 22% above economic rents, supported by tight vacancy. However, this margin is expected to be eroded in the coming years by rising financing costs and capitalisation rates, resulting in viability turning negative from 2030 onwards.

Sydney has the largest feasibility gap in Apac, which market rents currently 24% below economic rents. In addition to labour shortages and higher material and freight costs, pipelines for housing, infrastructure and and data centre developments are crowding out commercial projects, adding hurdles for new office development, say Cushman & Wakefield.

On the flipside, Seoul’s office market is expected to stay viable, thanks to steady demand underpinned by growing AI-related investment and strong semiconductor exports. In 2026, prime office rent in the South Korean capital stood 26% more than economic rent, with 20.7 million sq ft of office space currently under construction.

While the gap between market rent and economic rent is expected to narrow to 6% by 2030 and 5% and 2035 due to rising capitalisation rates, resilient demand is expected to keep the office market viable for new projects.

Similarly, new office developments in India’s Bengaluru are expected to be feasible through to 2035. Prime market rents, which currently sit at 16% above economic rents, are expected to grow 5% annually, outpacing economic rent growth of 2.5% per year.

Amid the divergent Apac office landscape, occupiers will have to tailor real estate strategies according to the market, says Anshul Jain, head of Apac offices and retail at Cushman & Wakefield.

“Organisations that actively review their portfolio strategies and have a clear view of local market dynamics will be better positioned to manage costs and secure quality space that support their long-term office needs,” he says.

title: Developers' sales rebound to 1,716 units in October, the year's highest monthly total
article:
Developers sold 1,716 new private homes, excluding executive condominiums (ECs), in October, according to data published by URA on Nov 16. That is 5.8 times the 296 units sold in September but 29.2% lower than the 2,424 units sold in October 2025.

It is the highest monthly sales volume of 2026, and the highest since October last year, noted Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip.

The rebound followed two subdued months, with 153 units sold in August and 296 in September.

SRI’s head of research and data analytics, Mohan Sandrasegeran, noted that the stronger sales were “largely anticipated”, as developers introduced their final wave of launches for the year.

Get the latest details on available units and prices for Lucerne Grand

These included the 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve , the 575-unit Lucerne Grand and the 133-unit The Serra Residences , plus additional units released at Dunearn House .

Overall, developers launched 2,058 units in October, over 13 times September’s 158 units but 7.8% lower than a year ago. This was the highest monthly launch volume of 2026 and the highest since October 2025, when 2,233 units were launched, added Sandrasegeran.

Thomson Reserve leads, Lucerne Grand follows

Top-selling projects in October 2026

Thomson Reserve was the top-selling project in October. The development, located on Bright Hill Drive in the Rest of Central Region (RCR), sold 1,029 units, or about 81%, at a median price of $2,865 psf during the month. That is also roughly 60% of all new private home sales (excluding ECs) in October.

The performance makes Thomson Reserve “possibly one of the best-selling projects in the RCR ever”, said Huttons’ Yip. He put the strong response down to the project’s pricing, which was “in line with market conditions”.

Yip added that for the entire third quarter of this year, Thomson Reserve’s sales alone were equivalent to 87% of the 1,180 new homes sold.

Sandrasegeran of SRI said the project’s sales suggest large-scale developments, especially those with good transport links and extensive facilities, continue to draw strong buyer interest. He cited the project’s proximity to the Thomson-East Coast Line, as well as the amenities and schools in the Upper Thomson neighbourhood.

He also noted that the return of major launches may have drawn back buyers who had been taking a measured approach during the quieter period in August and September.

Christine Sun, chief researcher and strategist at Realion (Orangetee & ETC) Group, pointed out that Thomson Reserve is the first mega-condo launch in the Upper Thomson neighbourhood since Jadescape in 2018. Limited supply in the area may have led to significant pent-up demand for private housing, she said.

The second best-selling project in October was Lucerne Grand, located in Jurong West in the Outside Central Region (OCR). The first project in the Lakeside precinct in 10 years, it sold 393 of its 570 units at a median of $2,496 psf during the month.

Close to 80% of units at Lucerne Grand were sold for less than $2.5 million, which Yip called the “sweet spot” price for OCR buyers.

The Serra Residences, a freehold District 11 project near the HealthCity Novena integrated healthcare hub, sold 25 units at a median of $3,311 psf, including one penthouse in October.

Other bestsellers for the month included Union Square Residences (41 units at $2,869 psf), Dunearn House (27 units at $3,108 psf) and Lentor Gardens Residences (21 units at $2,414 psf).

Beyond the new launches, Leonard Tay, head of research at Knight Frank Singapore, observed that sales activity in many existing projects remained relatively modest in October.

This indicates that while buyers are still participating in the market, they are being more discerning and “may be increasingly focused on developments that offer scale for a stronger value proposition”, Tay said.

Such increasing selectivity is not solely due to pricing or project attributes, as buyers are also weighing wider economic considerations, including the possibility of higher financing costs in the near future and evolving employment prospects.

These factors are likely influencing purchasers to be more measured as they pay more attention to affordability, financial resilience and a project’s overall value proposition, he added.

RCR takes two-thirds of sales; Singaporeans dominate

By region, the RCR or city fringe made up 67.4% of October new private home sales, followed by the OCR or suburbs at 28.4% and the CCR at 4.1%.

The RCR, where Thomson Reserve is situated, saw 1,157 new homes transacted, up significantly from 131 units in the previous month. According to PropNex, this was also the region’s highest monthly sales tally since October 2025, when 1,225 units were sold.    The OCR similarly put in a strong showing in October, with developers selling 488 new homes, the segment’s highest volume since April 2026, when 1,358 units were transacted.

PropNex CEO Kelvin Fong noted that sales in the OCR could likely pick up in 1Q2027, when more projects are slated to be launched. They include Chencharu Central Residences in Yishun, One Chuan Grove, and Lentor Signature.   Over in the CCR, 71 new units (excluding ECs) were transacted in October, up from the 40 units sold in September. The best-performing CCR project in the month was Dunearn House, which shifted 27 units at a median price of $3,108 psf, Fong said.

He added there are no further major CCR new launches till 1Q2027, when The River Opus may potentially be launched.

By absolute value, the top new home sale of the month was for a detached house in Bournemouth Road in the Katong-Mounbatten area of District 15. It was purchased by a Singaporean for $15.7 million.

Other highest-priced transactions in October included a penthouse at The Serra Residences that was sold to a permanent resident for $11.2 million, and a semi-detached house on Woo Mon Chew Road bought by a Singaporean for $10.4 million.

Executive condo sales continue to be sluggish

Developers sold 15 EC units at a median of $1,829 psf last month, falling 34.8% m-o-m from 23 units in September.

“This marks the segment’s weakest monthly performance since August, when just 18 new EC units were sold,” ERA Singapore CEO Marcus Chu said, adding that this was due to the lack of major new launches.

Fong of PropNex likewise pointed to the dwindling new EC stock in the market which contributed to the muted activity.

Coastal Cabana led transactions for the fifth consecutive month, with 14 units sold at a median of $1,820 psf, while Rivelle Tampines , which launched in March, accounted for the only other unit sold.

URA figures show only 137 new EC units from launched projects were left unsold as at the end of October.

“The tight supply of unsold EC units bodes well for the new EC launches,” Fong said.

In December, City Development Limited’s ( CDL ) 430-unit Wynwood Grand , the first EC in Woodlands since 2014, will open for e-applications, though bookings will only commence in January 2027.

Wynwood Grand will also be among the last few projects to offer a five-year minimum occupation period and access to the deferred payment scheme, said ERA’s Chu.

And in 2027, EC buyers can look forward to Solano Grand along Senja Close, Clovelle in Woodlands, and two yet-unnamed projects on Sembawang Road and Miltonia Close.

“Together with Wynwood Grand, these represent an injection of almost 2,000 new units into the EC market next year,” Chu noted.

Quiet end to the year expected

For the first 10 months of 2026, developers are estimated to have sold 7,053 new homes, 31.5% fewer than the 10,299 units in the same period last year, according to Huttons’ Yip.

In terms of launch volume, the year-to-date total comes up to an estimated 6,825 units offered for sale, down 38.4% y-o-y from 11,083.

Going into the year-end, sales are likely to settle into a “more measured pace” as the holiday season approaches, said SRI’s Sandrasegeran. Developers typically hold back launches while buyers may defer decisions because of year-end travel and festivities.

Yip expects only one private residential launch in November: the 43-unit luxury freehold The Park Residence on Stevens Road, featuring large-format homes of more than 4,000 sq ft. As such, he foresees developers’ sales falling to around 200 to 300 units for November.

Yip predicts new private home sales of up to 7,400 units for the whole of 2026, with 6,900 units launched. This would make it the first time since 2022 that developers have sold more compared to units launched. He estimates prices to rise 3% to 4% this year.

Looking ahead to 2027, Realion’s Sun said around 16,800 new private homes, or about 14,800 units if excluding ECs, could be released across more than 30 launch-ready projects.

This would mark the highest number of units entering the market since 2013, when 15,885 units were launched.

According to Sun, projects to watch include Hougang Central Residences, which will be part of an integrated development, as well as the Government Land Sales sites at Bayshore Drive and Dunearn Road Plot 2.

title: Westlite Dormitory to buy 3 Kim Chuan Lane for $61 million
article:
The freehold, eight-storey industrial building at 3 Kim Chuan Lane — also known as Goodland Group Building — in the Tai Seng-Kim Chuan precinct could soon change hands for $61 million in a proposed transaction, said the marketing agent Knight Frank Singapore on Nov 16.

That is 16.4% lower than the asking price of $73 million when the property was put up for sale via private treaty in August this year.

The seller, Goodland Development, wholly owned by Singapore-listed property developer Goodland Group, has inked the sale and purchase agreement on Nov 13 with the buyer, Westlite Dormitory (S III).

Westlite is the workers' accommodation brand of Singapore-listed Centurion Corporation.

The transaction will enable Goodland Group to unlock capital from a long-held industrial property while it retains an indirect, non-controlling investment in the asset through a separate joint-venture arrangement, said Knight Frank, without elaborating on the arrangement.

This structure provides Goodland Group with continued exposure to the property’s future income generation and potential long-term capital appreciation, the marketing agent added.

The proposed sale is expected to be completed by March 31, 2027, subject to the fulfilment of conditions under the agreement, including the necessary third-party and regulatory consents.

Completed in 2014, the development has 15 strata-titled factory units and two levels of basement car parking.

The purchase price works out to around $3,656 psf based on the Business 2 site area of some 16,685 sq ft, or about $1,110 psf if going by the total strata area of 54,939 sq ft.

The property has obtained planning approval for addition and alteration (A&A) works for food factory use, as well as outline planning permission for its proposed use as an independent workers’ dormitory.

"These provide alternative pathways for repositioning the asset, subject to the relevant regulatory requirements and further approvals where applicable," said Knight Frank Singapore.

Melvin Chay, interim head of capital markets at the firm, noted that 3 Kim Chuan Lane attracted strong interest, as opportunities with planning support for independent workers’ dormitory use are limited in the market.

Investors have shown growing interest in workers' accommodation, amid recurring income potential and sustained demand for dormitory beds.

The average occupancy was 95.8% for a basket of Class 4 purpose-built dormitories (those with 1,000 beds and above), while monthly bed rents rose 2.1% to $495 per bed, according to the 1H2026 research report jointly published by the Dormitory Association of Singapore Limited and Knight Frank Singapore.

At the same time, upcoming upgrading requirements for existing dormitories may also temporarily constrain available bed supply, the consultancy said.

Dayna Ang, senior manager of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore, described the Singapore industrial property market as resilient, with investment sales rising by 40.3% q-o-q to $2 billion in the third quarter of 2026.

"Building on our successful collective sale of 153 Kampong Ampat , this transaction [for 3 Kim Chuan Lane] reinforces sustained investor appetite for freehold industrial assets in a predominantly leasehold market, particularly those offering opportunities for redevelopment and value creation," she added.

title: Record $1.818 mil sale of Dawson flat: A bold asking price, 120 enquiries and five months of marketing
article:
Within weeks of being listed for sale, a five-room HDB flat at SkyParc @ Dawson in Queenstown had already attracted offers exceeding $1.7 million.

It would take roughly five months before the flat changed hands for $1.818 million , smashing the islandwide HDB resale record for the highest transaction price at the time of writing.

Along the way, the listing generated an estimated 120 enquiries and 40 to 50 viewings, with more than eight offers received.

"The response was very strong right from the start, which showed that our pricing framework was validated by the market," says Ted Wong of ERA Realty Network, who represented the sellers.

"Many of the enquirers were keen but did not manage to view in the end as the asking price, launched at the high $1.8 million range, was beyond their budgets."

In an interview with EdgeProp Singapore , Wong shares how securing such a record-breaking price involved more than showcasing the flat's high floor, sweeping greenery views, and an efficient and spacious layout.

Situated on the 40th to 42nd storeys of Block 96 Dawson Road , the unit measures about 1,194 sq ft in floor area and has a long remaining lease of around 94 years.

SkyParc @ Dawson was completed in 2020 with the 99-year lease tenure starting in 2021. The development houses 810 flats, with two- to five-room layouts, across three blocks ranging from 34 to 43 storeys. It also features landscaped communal spaces and sky gardens.

By absolute quantum, the Oct 30 sale was the first time a resale flat crossed the $1.8 million mark — far surpassing the previous all-time high of $1.728 million when a five-room flat at Block 96A Henderson Road, within City Vue @ Henderson in Bukit Merah, was resold in April 2026.

On a psf basis, the latest SkyParc unit's $1,522 psf price tag ranks as the second-highest for resale flats in Singapore.

The current all-time record remains $1,553 psf, set at The Pinnacle @ Duxton along Cantonment Road on Oct 7. That involved a 1,022 sq ft, four-room flat on the 28th to 30th storeys, which went for $1.588 million.

The $1.818 million SkyParc transaction incurred an undisclosed cash over valuation (COV) amount. Given the record-setting price, Wong had informed all viewers that they should expect a "reasonable" COV with the purchase.

"From the number of offers received, the COV clearly didn't diminish the demand and value buyers saw in the unit," he says.

Finer details behind the price premium

Wong was already familiar with Dawson and the wider Queenstown neighbourhood when the listing came to him through a personal referral.

"Having lived in this estate, I recognised the rare qualities of this flat," he says.

Besides the floor level, unit size, orientation, convenience and healthy balance lease, he also picked up on a less obvious feature that could appeal to buyers who want more privacy.

The flat is one of just four on its floor, compared with eight on most other levels. This lower density, found on the 39th to 43rd storeys of the block, offers an added sense of exclusivity.

"These are micro-USPs [unique selling points] which are not always obvious on standard property-portal listings," he says, adding that deep research and hyper-local familiarity enabled him to identify, prove and articulate those strengths to prospective buyers.

Wong, who has been a real estate salesperson for about four years, has brokered several million-dollar HDB deals alongside condo and landed home transactions. The HDB towns he knows best include prime clusters like Queenstown, Bukit Merah and Tiong Bahru.

To determine a suitable asking price for the SkyParc flat, he studied past transactions involving comparable units in the Central Region and other existing city-fringe listings.

Taking into account the flat’s unique attributes, he set an asking price in the high $1.8 million range.

"While the range may seem high to some, I was confident that it’s entirely justified," Wong says, pointing to the flat's USPs and the relative scarcity of five-room flats in the area.

He aims to be ambitious with pricing, but also realistic about what buyers are prepared to pay. An overly high asking price could leave a property languishing on the market until the listing becomes stale.

"Pricing is both an art and a science," he shares.

What makes homebuyers tick

Understanding the lifestyles and preferences of buyers looking for million-dollar homes in prime locations also helped tailor the marketing strategy.

Many buyers in non-central areas tend to prioritise living near extended family, their children’s schools and heartland amenities such as wet markets, Wong observes. Others simply want to return to neighbourhoods they grew up in.

On the other hand, those looking at newer HDB flats in the Central Region often place greater value on shorter commutes to work and the city, together with privacy, views and spaciousness.

They may see such flats as "a reasonably priced alternative to private condos", Wong notes.

In Dawson, the buyer pool he has come across for large flats includes affluent young families keen to move closer to the city centre, rightsizers from private property, as well as high-earning young professionals in finance, technology and law who want to live near their workplaces in the CBD.

With these groups in mind, he tailored the marketing in line with what they were most likely to appreciate.

"For example, marketing the fact that the flat is near Queenstown Primary School or Crescent Girls' School will usually be far less effective for this buyer pool," Wong says.

"In contrast, highlighting that it's within walking distance to lifestyle dining options at Dempsey Hill, or that they can get to their CBD office in 20 minutes, door to door, will carry more weight," Wong says.

For the SkyParc flat, he also staggered private viewing appointments with ample time between each slot.

This gave potential buyers a chance to take in the quiet surroundings, generous space and greenery views at their own pace.

He felt this approach was more suitable for the flat than a crowded open house, which can be more effective for homes in other estates.

"Most of the feedback from prospective buyers was about the grand view and efficient liveable space," Wong says.

Many viewers also commented that finding a home of this size, age and location under $3 million in the private residential market today would be "close to impossible", he adds.

Looking beyond past transactions

Despite the strong interest, not everyone was convinced that the SkyParc flat warranted more than $1.8 million — still an untested price point then.

Many prospective buyers and co-broking agents "naturally started with scepticism", especially when they simply compared the asking price with historical transaction trends rather than evaluating the flat's unique attributes, Wong says.

On top of showcasing the physical space, he walked buyers through the broader market factors influencing the demand and supply of HDB homes in Dawson, as well as the features that set the flat apart from nearby properties.

Demand for large flats in Dawson remains resilient, and five-room flats are "relatively low in supply" in the Central Region, Wong notes.

His own analysis and database of the Dawson market indicate that five-room flats make up an estimated 10.7% of about 5,100 units across the newer public housing projects there — namely Dawson Vista , SkyParc, SkyTerrace , SkyVille , SkyResidence and SkyOasis .

Another factor, which Wong says is often overlooked, is that Dawson stands as one of the last clusters of high-rise, city-fringe HDB projects to have recently completed their minimum occupation period (MOP), without being subject to the stricter rules for Plus and Prime flats.

Unlike homes under these classifications, the newly MOP-ed flats in Dawson are not subject to a 10-year MOP, subsidy clawback or tighter resale and rental conditions.

This means homeowners may have more flexibility and a wider pool of future buyers. "In my view, it could partially explain the price tear between HDB flats in prime areas versus those in the suburbs," Wong says.

"My personal take is that this structural market difference has not been fully priced in, and therein lies opportunities for buyers who are able to recognise it."

These longer-term and macro-level considerations informed his approach to marketing the SkyParc flat.

He aimed to shift the viewers’ perspective from focusing on recent transactions to also thinking about possible future scarcity, as he reckons real estate pricing can be forward-looking.

Although historical data offers a useful reference, he believes it does not always capture the premium that buyers may be willing to pay for a property that is difficult to find elsewhere.

"If agents solely look at past transactions, the client’s upside is capped," he says.

"By seeing the flat as a unique asset amid a limited supply, we can enable true price discovery. This is often clearer in the landed property market, where supply is tight and land plots are unique."

Turning keen interest into a record sale

The strategy gained traction early on, with offers above $1.7 million coming in within the first few weeks of marketing, though Wong did not rush to close a deal.

He gave qualified buyers a clear timeline to submit their best offers, which allowed him to guide negotiations towards the eventual $1.818 million sale without prolonging the process and risking buyer fatigue.

Of the more than eight offers received in approximately five months, three exceeded $1.8 million.

Interested parties were attracted to the city-fringe location, abundant amenities nearby, unblocked verdant vistas and generous floor area.

Wong expects the transacted price to establish a new benchmark for exceptional high-floor, five-room units in the Central Region.

"My view is that this will not be an isolated case," he notes.

That said, a Dawson address alone will not guarantee a similarly high price. Wong points out that achieving a record-breaking price also depends on how a property is positioned and marketed, how sellers’ expectations are managed and how negotiations with qualified buyers are handled.

Reflecting on the sale, Wong says he is glad to have delivered a satisfactory outcome for the sellers.

"At the end of the day, I’m deeply grateful for the trust they placed in me to market their home."

title: Castlery's third Australian showroom lands in Melbourne
article:
Singapore-founded furniture brand Castlery has opened its first showroom in Melbourne, marking its debut in Victoria and the next step in its Australian retail expansion.

The showroom at 6 Yorkshire Street in Richmond opened its doors on Oct 29, with an official grand opening event that followed on Nov 14 and 15.

The single-level showroom measures 448 sq m (4,822 sq ft) and features 17 curated room sets, including one styled by Castlery’s Australian brand ambassador Steve Cordony.

It is Castlery’s fifth showroom globally and third in Australia, following its Sydney debut in June 2024 and the opening of its Brisbane showroom in August 2025. The retailer also expanded the Sydney showroom in December 2025.

“Melbourne has been two years in the making for us. We knew we wanted to be here, but finding the right location mattered,” said Leah Howatson, general manager of international markets at Castlery.

“Australia was Castlery’s first international market, and as we approach 10 years in Australia next year, opening our third Australian showroom represents another important step in putting down deeper roots here.”

Howatson added that with Castlery already in more than 60,000 Melbourne homes, the company wanted a location that would bring it closer to customers while placing it within the city’s design community.

The showroom’s design takes its cues from Melbourne’s heritage. A faux skylight in the lobby and the adjoining timber shelving pay homage to the reading room of State Library Victoria, Australia’s oldest public library.

Timber panelling behind the reception counter draws from Melbourne’s brick warehouse architecture, and a red marble counter complements the palette .

Existing beams, once painted black, have been stripped back to reveal the original timber underneath.

Castlery’s signature design features, carried through from its Sydney and Brisbane showrooms, tie the space together.

“Melbourne has a special way of bringing old and new together, with homes that feel layered and collected over time rather than designed all at once,” said Howatson.

The showroom also offers Castlery’s complimentary interior styling service, which gives customers one-on-one sessions with in-store stylists for advice on styling and product recommendations.

Founded in Singapore in 2013, Castlery serves customers in the US, UK, Australia, Singapore and Canada.

title: Is the Great Singapore REIT Comeback Finally Here?
article:
Singapore
real estate investment trusts
(REITs) have had a frustrating couple of years.
The
iEdge S-REIT Index
(SGX: SRU) was down about 14.1% year to date as at 13 November 2026 against the
Straits Times Index’s
(SGX: ^STI) 12.3% gain.
Yet, some REITs are quietly growing their distributions again.
So, is this the start of a proper recovery or just a pause before the next leg down?
The answer depends on more than interest rates.
Why Singapore REITs Have Struggled and What’s Different Now
Higher interest rates
did most of the damage.
When rates went up, REITs had to refinance their loans at higher costs, leaving less to pay out as distributions per unit (DPU).
Meanwhile, income investors could earn a decent return from T-bills and fixed deposits without taking any risk.
Some REITs also struggled with falling property values or weak overseas performance, while banks and growth stocks pulled money away.
Some of that pressure is lifting.
Local interest rates have eased, so older loans are being refinanced more cheaply.
Singapore offices and malls are signing leases at higher rents, occupancy rates are still firm, and many REITs still trade below their net asset value (NAV).
If these trends hold, the three REITs below could benefit.

Suntec looks the most defensive, NTT DC REIT has the clearest growth, and SET offers the highest yield for those willing to take on more risk.
Suntec REIT (SGX: T82U) – Strong Rents That Benefit From Lower Rates
Suntec REIT is best known for Suntec City, and it also owns stakes in One Raffles Quay and Marina Bay Financial Centre.
Outside Singapore, it has offices in Australia and the UK.
Business at home is going well.
As at 30 September 2026 (3Q2026), its Singapore offices were 99.6% occupied and its malls 98.6%.
In 3Q2026, rental reversions were 7.3% for its Singapore offices and 11.2% for its malls.
DPU for the first nine months (9M2026) rose 20.7% year on year (YoY), helped by lower interest costs.
At a unit price of S$1.35 as at 13 November 2026, Suntec REIT offers a trailing distribution yield of 6.0% and trades at about 0.66x its net asset value (NAV) of S$2.04 per unit.
The main weakness is debt.
Gearing climbed to 43.0%, and an interest coverage ratio (ICR) of 2.3x.
Its all-in financing cost has fallen to 3.57%, from 3.71% at 31 December 2025.
Should Suntec manage to sell its three Australian assets, gearing could improve from current levels.
Management expects future DPU growth to be from higher Singapore rents and lower financing costs.
The main risks for Suntec would likely be from its overseas holdings and higher financing costs.
NTT DC REIT (SGX: NTDU) – The Growth Recovery Play
This data centre REIT owns six properties in the US, Austria, and Singapore.
That’s a rare corner of property where rents are still climbing at a healthy clip.
Its maiden DPU, ending 31 March 2026 (FY2025/2026), came in at US$0.0556.
At a unit price of US$0.945 as at 13 November 2026, this works out to an estimated distribution yield of 5.9%.
Do note this distribution covered less than a full year.
For the first quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2026/2027), portfolio occupancy was 95.9% (rising to 99.2% once signed leases start), and renewals were signed at rents 13.4% higher.
The balance sheet leaves plenty of room for acquisition-fuelled growth.
Gearing is at 31%, while its ICR stands at 4.7x.
No loans fall due for two years, and the REIT has US$261 million of debt headroom before it reaches its 40% gearing limit.
The main risks include rising power costs, 14% of rent that’s up for renewal in this financial year, and a concentrated tenant base where the top 10 pay 74.5% of rent.
Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust (SGX: SET) – The High-Yield Opportunity
Stoneweg Europe, or SET, owns mostly logistics and office properties across Europe.
At a unit price of €1.50 as at 13 November 2026, it yields about 9.0% and trades at roughly 0.74x NAV.
The distribution looks steady for now.
Distribution per stapled security (DPS) rose 1.4% to €0.0664 in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), and management expects the full-year figure to be broadly in line with FY2025.
Logistics rental reversion was 9.6%, with a healthy occupancy rate of 95.2%, so why are the units trading near 52-week lows?
Offices are the drag.
Occupancy is only at 90.3%, and office rental reversion was down 4.1%.
Gearing looks manageable at 41.9%, with an ICR of 3.0x.
Crucially, 90% of its debt is hedged, and there’s no major refinancing until 2030.
This gives the REIT some time before its office segment recovers.
SET is also moving into data centres, which could provide some potential upside, but this brings execution risk.
On balance, the yield is tempting, but you’re being paid to accept weaker office performance and a big strategy shift (into data centres).
What Could Stop the REIT Comeback?
Another Fed rate hike, or rates that stay elevated, would keep refinancing costs up.
Weaker rents, further declines in property values or fresh DPU cuts would also hurt.
Finally, the continued preference for
banks
, risk-free income alternatives, or growth stocks could keep investors away from REITs.
Cheap REITs can stay cheap if the reasons behind the discount don’t change.
Get Smart: A Recovery Worth Watching
S-REITs could be close to a turning point, though a lot still depends on where interest rates go.
And even if sentiment picks up, some REITs will recover much faster than others.
The ones to look for have growing rents and debt that’s under control, because those are the REITs most able to raise DPU.
Investors who focus on these qualities may be well placed if the sector’s recovery takes hold.

title: Record Fees at UOB and iFAST: Where Singapore’s Wealth Is Flowing

This earnings season, the bigger story sat one line above the payout.
Two Singapore-listed financial companies set records in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026).

iFAST Corporation Ltd
(SGX: AIY) ended the quarter with a record S$36.8 billion in assets under administration (AUA).
Here’s the thing: both records arrived while bank lending margins shrank.
UOB’s net interest margin (NIM) narrowed to 1.68% from 1.82% a year ago.
At
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05), NIM fell to 1.87% from 1.96%.
Why should you care?
Banks earn fees on the money they manage and the services they sell, so fee income ties up less capital than lending.
Fee income also depends less on interest rates.
So which of these three companies turns fee growth into dividends most directly?

How much of iFAST’s growth keeps coming back?
iFAST

Its AUA rose 20.0% year on year (YoY) to a record S$36.8 billion.
Clients added S$1.24 billion of net inflows, and rising markets helped too.

Recurring net revenue grew 22.0% YoY to S$95.4 million, which made up 86.2% of net revenue.
Net profit attributable to owners rose 24.5% YoY to S$32.4 million.
And shareholders are getting a bigger slice.
The third interim dividend rose 39.1% YoY to S$0.0320.
Management expects a FY2026 dividend of at least S$0.1200, above its April 2026 guidance of S$0.1050.
On the flip side, iFAST now carries more debt.
Borrowings, excluding lease liabilities, rose to S$234.3 million from S$113.1 million at the end of 2025.
A S$120 million note issue in March 2026 accounts for most of the increase.
Can DBS’s fees make up for a weak trading quarter?
DBS serves retail, wealth and corporate customers across Asia.
Its customer businesses kept growing.
Net fee and commission income rose 6% YoY to S$1.43 billion, and treasury customer sales and other income grew 19% to S$685 million.
Trading was a different story.
Markets trading non-interest income fell to S$17 million from S$419 million a year ago.
Net profit for the quarter dropped 4.8% to S$2.81 billion.
To be sure, one weak quarter doesn’t undo the year.
Net profit for the first nine months of 2026 reached a record S$8.82 billion.
The dividend comes in two parts, so read them separately.
DBS declared an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share and a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share.
The S$0.81 total is 8% higher than the S$0.75 paid a year ago.
Management expects structural growth in wealth management to continue.
For 2027, it guides for total income growth in the mid-single-digit range.
Is UOB’s record fee haul enough to lift its payout?
UOB
serves more than 8 million customers across the region.
Its net fee income rose 19% YoY to the record S$733 million, with wealth, cards and loan-related activities driving the gain.
The rest of the bank had a tougher quarter.
Other non-interest income fell 29% to S$370 million on lower trading and investment income.
Operating profit before allowances declined 2.8% to S$1.8 billion, while total expenses rose 2%.
If you’re waiting for a dividend, it’s not due yet.
UOB pays dividends twice a year, so it declared none this quarter.
That’s a matter of timing, not a cut.
Look closer at the 2027 guidance.
UOB expects fee income to grow at a mid- to high-single-digit pace and operating costs to rise at a similar rate.
If both forecasts hold, fees alone won’t widen the gap between income and costs.
UOB says it is investing in capital-light businesses that broaden its sources of revenue.
Get Smart: Follow the fees, then follow the payout
A record fee number is a good start.
But it doesn’t tell you how much of that money reaches you.
When the next set of results arrives, check whether the fee line is growing faster than costs.
Then check whether the dividend follows.
iFAST’s recurring revenue and its dividend are both rising today.
DBS has raised its total payout.

title: Jensen Huang Resigns: What NVIDIA’s CEO Exit Teaches You About Key-Man Risk
article:
NVIDIA
(NASDAQ: NVDA) lost a key co-founder last week.
Jensen Huang built the
chipmaker
over 33 years.
On 12 November 2026, he resigned as chief executive officer with immediate effect.
He also left the board.
There are no prizes for guessing why.
But what about investors?
A line often attributed to
Warren Buffett
fits the moment.
“I try to invest in businesses that are so wonderful that an idiot can run them. Because sooner or later, one will.”
Let me be clear: Jensen Huang is no idiot.
He has, however, left some big shoes to fill.
A great company should keep its edge after its founder walks out the door.
What happens at NVIDIA now?
Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s chief financial officer, is now interim CEO.
She will be at the helm until the board names a permanent successor.
Harvey C. Jones, a former chief executive of chip-design software firm
Synopsys
(NASDAQ: SNPS), becomes the board’s first-ever chair.
The board will consider internal and external candidates, and it has not set a timeline.
As you can tell, there are many open questions.
You can expect analysts to have a field day when NVIDIA reports its third-quarter results on 17 November 2026, as scheduled.
Jones said the company expects its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap “to continue without interruption”.
Why does one departure matter so much?
Huang ran NVIDIA unlike most chief executives.
He had about 60 direct reports, and he skipped one-on-one meetings in favour of group sessions.
That set-up let decisions move fast.
It also meant much of NVIDIA’s judgement rested on one person.
In the near term, demand for AI chips may carry the business.
The harder test comes later, when NVIDIA’s next leader has to pick the company’s big long-term bets without him.
How can you spot key-man risk in your own portfolio?
NVIDIA is listed in the US, but SGX companies can carry the same risk.
You can
check for it
in your own holdings.
Look at who chairs the board.
An independent chair who is not the CEO gives the board a voice of its own. NVIDIA named its first chair in the same announcement as Huang’s exit.
Read the management pages of the annual report.
A deep bench of senior executives with long tenures gives the board people it can promote from within.
Search for succession planning.
The corporate governance report should explain how the nominating committee plans for a change of CEO. A vague answer or missing statement is a signal too.
Ask where the advantage sits.
An edge built on assets, contracts, or customer relationships lasts longer than one built on a single person’s judgement.
Get Smart: Own the business, not the boss
A great leader is a good reason to like a stock.
It should not be your only reason.
Before you buy, ask yourself this: if the CEO resigned tomorrow, would you still want to own the shares?
If your answer is no, your investment case rests on one person.
Size your position with that in mind.

title: How to Balance REIT Dividends with US Growth Stocks for Maximum Returns
article:
Ask the people around you how they want to grow their wealth, and the answer is usually one of two things: steady dividends or capital appreciation.
And the go-to is usually Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs) for the former and US tech giants for the latter.
However, going all-in on either means taking on all of its weak spots.
When you mix REITs with
US growth stocks
, you strike a balance between consistent cash flow and long-term upside.
Here’s how to make them work together.
Why Combine REITs and US Growth Stocks?
REITs own
income-generating properties
like malls and warehouses, collect rent, and pay out 90%+ of taxable income for corporate tax breaks.
That high payout makes them an income favourite.
Reinvest the payout, and watch your money snowball faster.
On the flip side, big tech stalwarts like
Microsoft Corporation
(NASDAQ: MSFT),
Alphabet Inc
(NASDAQ: GOOGL), and
Amazon.com Inc
(NASDAQ: AMZN) skip the hefty payouts and pour their cash directly into expansion, especially AI and cloud infrastructure.
They run on entirely different engines.
Blending them gives you sensible diversification, but don’t treat it like a bulletproof hedge.
When a sharp sell-off strikes, both can easily drop at the same time.
Choosing the Right Singapore REITs for Dividend Income
A fat yield means little if the payout behind it is shrinking.
So before buying a REIT, always check if its payout is growing.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), Singapore’s largest REIT, raised its distribution per unit (DPU) by 7.1% to S$0.0602 in 1H2026.
This was driven by strong rental reversions of 4.0% in retail and 6.5% in offices, alongside a resilient occupancy rate of 95.6%.
In contrast,
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U)’s 1HFY2026/2027 DPU slipped 5.7% to S$0.0608 after property sales and weaker occupancy at its North American portfolio.
A headline yield above 6% is definitely juicy, but a declining payout quickly erodes that initial appeal.
Balance sheet strength also plays a critical role.
When interest rates stay elevated, a REIT’s gearing directly impacts the bottom line.
CICT maintains a gearing ratio of 37.4% with an average cost of debt at 2.9%.
Healthcare pure-play
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU) runs even leaner at 33.8% gearing, helping power a 14.6% jump in its 1H2026 DPU on the back of rising Singapore hospital rents.
That’s why sector diversification matters too!
Malls, offices, hospitals, and warehouses all answer to different tenants, so a slump in one won’t sink your payouts.
Selecting US Growth Stocks for Long-Term Capital Appreciation
For a growth company to stay great, it needs something special, something rivals find hard to copy.
Companies like Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon have that kind of edge.
Microsoft reported 19.0% year-on-year (YoY) growth in revenue to US$92.3 billion for 1QFY2027, with its Azure cloud business up 48.0%.
Alphabet’s 3Q2026 revenue climbed 25.0% YoY to US$127.6 billion as Google Cloud revenue soared 103.0%.
Similarly, Amazon posted 12.0% YoY growth to US$201.9 billion for 3Q2026, as AWS sales were up 39.0%.
However, growth only counts if it eventually becomes free cash flow.
And here’s where the picture splits.
Over the past 12 months, Microsoft generated US$60.0 billion of free cash flow and Alphabet US$19.4 billion, although Alphabet’s quarterly free cash flow has dipped below zero in each of the last two quarters.
Meanwhile, Amazon swung to a negative US$42.4 billion as its AI spending ballooned.
That said, negative cash flow is not necessarily bad if those data centres pay off, but it is still a risk to watch.
How Much Should You Allocate to REITs vs US Growth Stocks?
There’s no perfect asset split for everyone.
It simply comes down to your age, goals, and how many ups and downs you can stomach.
If you’re close to retiring, locking in consistent cash flow and capital preservation takes priority.
But if you have decades ahead, you can ride out bigger swings for more growth.

The income-focused mix pays the most today and swings the least, but grows more slowly.

Remember, this two-asset combo is just a baseline model, not a complete portfolio.
You’ll still want an emergency cash cushion, some bond allocation for ballast, and broad-market shares outside of property and tech.
How Dividends and Growth Can Work Together
While you are building wealth, reinvest your REIT distributions into more units, or into
growth stocks
when their valuations look reasonable.
That helps rebalance your portfolio without selling anything.
As retirement nears, gradually shift towards income.
Let your stage of life drive the change and not the latest headlines.
What Are the Risks of Combining REITs and US Growth Stocks?
Interest rates are one of the most important risks to watch, as they cut both ways.
Higher rates raise REIT borrowing costs and tend to drag down growth-stock prices too.
Currency is another.
As US stocks are priced in US dollars, if the greenback weakens against the Singapore dollar, your returns shrink when converted back.
Also, watch out for concentration.
Having three technology giants or five shopping malls is not diversification.
Lastly, volatility.
Both can drop 20% or more, so keep an emergency fund and you’ll never be forced to sell at the bottom.
How to Measure Whether Your Portfolio Is Working
Watch your total return – payouts plus price changes.
A 7% yielder whose unit price falls 10% has still lost you money.
Check that your REITs’ DPU rises over time and review your portfolio at least once a year.
If your mix drifts off target, rebalance based on business fundamentals, not price swings.
Get Smart: Balance Income Today with Growth Tomorrow
REITs pay you now while growth stocks build wealth for later.
Whatever the mix, judge each holding on payout quality, debt, and cash flow, not just its yield.
That goal is never to buy the biggest yield or hottest stock.
It’s simply to
build a portfolio
that delivers solid total returns and fits your life.

title: Wheat falls on optimism about Black Sea talks, Argentine supply
article:
(Nov 16): Wheat futures in Chicago fell on optimism about progress in negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict in the Black Sea and expectations of strong supplies from the Southern Hemisphere.

The most-active contract fell as much as 1.1%, though it later pared some of those losses. Hard red winter wheat also fell. US President Donald Trump is expected to meet with his Chinese and Russian counterparts later this week, with the escalation of tensions in the Black Sea expected to be discussed.

Persistent disruptions to shipping in the Black Sea have curbed wheat outflows from the key producing region, threatening supplies across Asia and Africa. Still, optimism about a resolution is tempered by continued attacks by both Russia and Ukraine.

“Russia-Ukraine fighting continues despite renewed peace negotiations,” said Joe Davis, a director of commodity sales at Futures International LLC. “This is keeping Black Sea shipping risks elevated.”

At the same time, the forecast for Argentina’s wheat crop was raised last week to 24.3 million tonnes, up from a previous estimate of 23.8 million tonnes.

Wheat prices are factoring in both the disruption to Black Sea export flows and abundant Southern Hemisphere supplies, CM Navigator analysts wrote in a note.

title: European gas dips as record US flows counter storage concerns
article:
(Nov 16): European natural gas fell as traders weighed record exports from the US against persistent concerns about the continent’s thin winter inventories.

Benchmark futures dropped as much as 6.2% on Monday after adding more than 6% last week. Milder weather is set to spread across Europe in the coming days — potentially limiting heating demand — while more supply is coming to the global market from the US after projects there increased production to a fresh peak.

In addition, near-term market tightness is easing as major importers in Asia remain on the sidelines, according to traders.

Still, more cold spells are expected in Europe later this month, while supply disruptions continue in the Middle East. Europe’s gas-storage sites are less than 71% full, well below the five-year seasonal average of 89%, exposing the region to more price spikes when freezing weather sets in.

“The market is very much tied to volatility as winter demand bites while the supply side looks to improve,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank.

See also: US diesel falls below US$6 a gallon, easing key inflationary pressure

In the UK, gas has begun flowing from the recently approved Jackdaw project. While the field is a relatively minor contribution to the market — at about 2% of Britain’s annual gas demand — the nation’s energy secretary said it will help boost supply security this winter.

Meanwhile, tensions in the Middle East continue. Over the weekend, Iran targeted a US base in Bahrain, even as it reiterated that a path to ending the conflict remains open. Attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have also continued. Gas prices in Europe are likely to remain elevated so long as the conflict remains unresolved.

“The winter balance remains sensitive to weather, supply disruptions and further shifts in market sentiment,” analysts at Timera Energy said in a note.

Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s gas benchmark, traded 5.3% lower at €86.10 a megawatt-hour by 1.41pm in Amsterdam.
